analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health insurance program financed by a new value-added tax.
analysis.headline: The national health insurance bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, drew zero cosponsors, and died without a hearing, markup, or vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a national health insurance program covering medical, dental, hospital, home-nursing, and other services for people who meet work-history requirements, letting patients freely choose their doctors and hospitals. It would be financed by a new value-added tax on commercial transactions — with food, housing, and medical care exempt — flowing into a National Health Care Trust Fund. Administration would be decentralized to states and local boards, with doctors paid by fee schedule, salary, or per-patient amounts and hospitals paid at cost. It never moved: after referral to two committees in January 1993, it sat in subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people and their families who meet the work-history test, retirees, and the uninsured needy (covered when public agencies reimburse the fund). Anyone facing large premiums, out-of-pocket costs, or denial of coverage under private insurance would gain guaranteed coverage with free choice of physician and hospital, no discrimination by race, creed, or color, and no premiums.

how_it_helps.text: Makes medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services available as benefits to eligible individuals, with full freedom to choose and change physicians and hospitals.

Declares the existing payment system — charity for the poor and 'unpredictable and often unbearable costs' for everyone else — unfixable by any voluntary insurance system, and establishes prepaid coverage on the principle of social insurance.
Sets the value-added tax rate at zero for retail food, principal-residence housing, and medical care, and prohibits discrimination on account of race, creed, or color in providing benefits.

Pays hospitals on the basis of reasonable cost and authorizes grants to train health personnel, with payments designed to encourage practitioners to serve localities where their services are most needed.
Requires that Federal Medicaid and related grants be usable by states to pay for covering noninsured needy individuals under the same program, on the same terms as everyone else.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and consumers pay the new value-added tax on commercial transactions, which replaces private premiums, employer coverage contributions, and most out-of-pocket costs. Doctors and hospitals accept Board-set payment rules, and private health insurers lose most of their role.
analysis.who_pays_short: Businesses paying the new tax; insurers

drawbacks.text: Coverage is not universal: eligibility rests on wage-history thresholds tied to quarters of work, and the uninsured needy are covered only when public agencies reimburse the fund for their care.

Hospital benefits are capped at 60 days per benefit year, exclude mental-disease hospitals, and stop 30 days after a psychosis diagnosis; the Board may also limit dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services whenever it finds personnel, facilities, or funds inadequate.
Seniors on Medicare initially receive only the services Medicare does not cover, with full merger of Medicare into the program deferred pending a study and future legislation.

A value-added tax, even with food, housing, and medical care zero-rated, still falls on consumption and would be a large new federal tax on businesses and households, and the bill gives the Board broad power to restrict services if the trust fund runs short.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would guarantee doctor-choice coverage to most Americans and abolish premiums and medical bills, a large direct gain for ordinary households, paid for by a broad new consumption tax whose heaviest burden falls on businesses. Its design tries to defuse the classic objections — patients keep free choice of physician, doctors keep fee-for-service options and the right to reject patients, and administration stays local — but the work-history eligibility rules leave out people outside the workforce, the 60-day hospital cap and service-limitation powers are real gaps, and financing the entire health system through one new tax was the core political obstacle.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, then to their health subcommittees, and nothing further ever happened to it.

narrative.text: John Dingell introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, the first day of the 103rd Congress, and it was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees.

On January 12, 1993 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and on February 16, 1993 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its two years on the books.
Benefits were to first become available October 1, 1994, but that date came and went with the bill still stalled in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and the existing employer-based insurance system, which continued unchallenged; the status quo also survived the rival Clinton administration reform effort in the same Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI) and chairman of the Energy and Commerce Committee; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 103rd Congress and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to the committee he chaired and to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee and its Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 5, 1993 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Health on January 12, 1993; scheduled no markup and never reported the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 5, 1993 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on February 16, 1993; no hearing or markup followed in the two years that remained.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Spent the 103rd Congress pushing its own managed-competition Health Security Act rather than endorsing a single-payer national insurance plan, leaving this bill without the White House behind it.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Health Insurance Association of America and allied insurers
against.what_they_did: Ran a major public campaign against government-run health coverage during the 1993-94 health reform fight, including the widely seen 'Harry and Louise' advertisements.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the sole sponsor was a Democrat, the bill drew zero cosponsors of either party, and the opposition that mattered was the Democratic White House's competing plan and the insurance industry rather than a recorded party split.

industries.note: A government trust fund paying providers directly would eliminate the core private insurance function; the bill lets voluntary health plans serve only as agents or administrators for the state program, not as gatekeepers. Insurers' revenue depends on the current system the bill would replace, and their interests ran against the uninsured and underinsured who would have gained coverage.

Employers would pay a new value-added tax on their commercial transactions, but would stop paying health premiums and no longer bear responsibility for covering workers. The bill shifts a cost businesses currently carry into a broad tax.

Hospitals would be paid reasonable cost for everyone they treat, ending uncompensated care for the uninsured, but the Board could cap hospitalization rates and payments would default to multiple-bed accommodations, squeezing hospitals that currently charge more. The bill forbids federal supervision of hospital personnel decisions.

The bill is deliberately built to keep doctors whole: free choice of locality, fee-for-service among the payment options, the right to reject patients, and no 'state medicine' salaried mandate. The main cost is that payment rates and specialist standards would be set by a federal Board rather than negotiated with insurers.

Prescribed drugs the Board designates as essential would be covered under a single public payer, which historically pays less than fragmented private coverage; unusually expensive drugs would be included only if the Board finds their provision practicable.
